_why: ADR 0027's mutation table, re-derived under scripts/mutate.py.
This is Barbara Bakker's feedback, and the record of how it was being
served wrong. She said a parameter's reliability should drive which
value gets used. Terrium implemented her three axes twice -- once in
Python, once in TypeScript -- with a parity test asserting the two
agreed on a shared fixture. They did agree. The API server called the
TypeScript grader with no PhysiologicalReference, because none was
reachable from an HTTP request, so `conditionProximity` returned
`not_assessed` on every response it ever produced.
Both graders return `not_assessed` with no reference. They agreed
perfectly, on a question neither was being asked.
The interesting row is R1. The duplicate grader was DELETED rather than
bypassed, and a deletion cannot be mutation-tested by removing something
-- there is nothing left to remove. It is tested by putting one BACK,
under a different name, which is exactly how a deleted duplicate returns
in practice: somebody needs a grade in TypeScript and writes a helper

mutations.description: reintroduce a grader under a different name
mutations._note: The deletion guard. `reliabilityScore.ts` is types only; the test asserts the module exports NO callable at all, rather than asserting the absence of one particular name -- which a rename would defeat.
